title: Drop repeats in a parallel stream without a shared seen-set

blocks.text: A filter whose lambda reads and writes shared state is *stateful*: its answer for one element depends on what the lambda saw before. In a parallel stream "before" means "on some thread, earlier in time", not "earlier in the list". `distinct()` is the stream's own stateful step: on an ordered stream it keeps the first occurrence of each element in encounter order, whatever the threads do.
Write `KeepFirst.firstOccurrences(Stream<Integer> ids)`. It returns each id once, at the place where it first occurs, in encounter order. The stream may be sequential or parallel.
The tests use ids whose first appearance is not their numeric order, and a large parallel stream in which every id appears twice.

cases.says: It keeps one copy of each id from a sequential stream.
The ids come back in the order they first appear, which collecting to a HashSet does not keep.
On a parallel stream each id is kept at its first occurrence: a shared seen-set keeps whichever copy a thread reaches first.
Equal ids above 127 are still repeats: two boxed Integers of 1000 are equal but not the same object.
A parallel stream of 19999 down to 0, twice, gives 19999 down to 0: encounter order, not sorted order.

origin.section: Common Pitfalls and How to Avoid Them

concepts: A filter that reads and writes a shared seen-set decides by thread timing; distinct keeps first occurrences in encounter order.
